newsitem.title: FRANCE: France plans new art controls, worries collectors.
newsitem.headline: France plans new art controls, worries collectors.

text.p: Paris is planning new art export controls to prevent masterpieces from slipping abroad, an official said on Tuesday, but sought to reassure collectors who fear restrictions might slash art prices in France.
"It's true that we're trying to keep a few works of national heritage in France, about two or three a year, and we will try to buy them," said Francoise Cachin, head of France's state-run museums.

"We're trying to improve (the law) and not abandon the previous principles. We will remain very liberal," she told Reuters, commenting on a report in the daily Liberation that Paris wanted to tighten the existing 1992 legislation.
Cachin said the text of a draft law would be ready within a month.

Auctioneers fear that the threat of new restrictions could prompt collectors to pack up their most precious works and flee before any legislation takes effect. Restrictions might also be unworkable with open European Union borders.
Cachin said details of the draft were not yet fixed but the principle of compensation for works declared "national treasures" would remain.

Liberation said the Ministry of Culture aimed to scrap the provision, scaring investors who know that a painting sold on the international market in New York or Tokyo can fetch far more than works limited to France.

In the most spectacular case, owners of Vincent Van Gogh's "Jardin a Auvers," one of the Dutch artist's last masterpieces painted in 1890, won 145 million francs ($29 million) from the French state under a court order when its export was banned.

Jacques Tajan, an auctioneer who tried to sell the "Jardin a Auvers" last month but failed when the top bid of 32 million francs ($6.4 million) fell short of the reserve price, said the government seemed to be blundering into legislation.
"Art collectors are very worried," he told Reuters. "No one has been consulted."

Tajan said a French art collector visited him on Monday for advice on whether it was better to take his paintings out of the country, or at least apply for export permits under the existing legislation.
"I think I would in his position," Tajan told Reuters. "If they're banned from leaving the country they will lose two-thirds of their value."
The current system has been widely criticised, especially because the payment over the "Jardin a Auvers", still in a private collection, gutted France's budget for new acquisitions.

Pierre Rosenberg, the director of the Louvre museum, said the 1992 law was "disastrous" because it had barred exports without giving museums the cash to buy new works. "The French heritage is threatened as never before," he told Liberation.

He noted that Rubens' "Decapitation of St John the Baptist" and Poussin's "Agony in the Garden of Olives" both recently left France. Just 39 works have been denied export permits out of 11,000 applications.
Tajan said restrictive laws did not work. "Italy is probably the most prohibitive country in Europe but people just smuggle works out. The law is so strict that no one asks for permits," he said.
